faqs.question: What emoji should I send to say I miss you?
faqs.answer: There is no emoji that means it, so pick by what the other person will read rather than by a list. 🫂 U+1FAC2 people hugging is the most literal, and 💔 U+1F494 broken heart is the one most likely to be over-read as a breakup.

faqs.question: What does 🥺 actually mean?
faqs.answer: Its CLDR short name is pleading face and its formal Unicode character name is FACE WITH PLEADING EYES, both meaning asking rather than missing. It was added in Unicode 11.0, released in 2018, so it will not show on a phone whose emoji font is older than that.

faqs.question: What does the 🫂 hugging emoji mean?
faqs.answer: 🫂 is U+1FAC2, CLDR short name people hugging, added in Unicode 13.0 in 2020. It has no faces, no gender and no skin tone, which is why it reads the same whether you send it to a partner or to a parent.

faqs.question: Is 💔 too strong for just missing someone?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. 💔 U+1F494 broken heart scores −0.121 in the Emoji Sentiment Ranking and carries breakup and bereavement meanings alongside ordinary absence, so a recipient has to guess which one you meant.

faqs.question: Why does the emoji I sent show up as a blank box on their phone?
faqs.answer: That box is called tofu, and it means their emoji font predates the character. 🥹 and 🫰 both need Unicode 14.0 from 2021, while 💔 😢 😭 😔 date to Unicode 6.0 in 2010 and render nearly everywhere.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🥹 and 😂?
faqs.answer: They are different characters. 🥹 is U+1F979, face holding back tears, added in Unicode 14.0; 😂 is U+1F602, face with tears of joy, from Unicode 6.0. Mixing the two names up is one of the most common errors in emoji explainers.

faqs.question: Does 😢 mean the person is actually sad?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. In the Emoji Sentiment Ranking 😢 scores +0.007 across 749 occurrences, with 39.1% of human annotations positive against 38.4% negative — statistically indistinguishable from neutral.

faqs.question: Do emoji mean something different to Gen Z?
faqs.answer: For a handful of emoji that have actually been tested, yes. A 2024 Language@Internet survey found Gen Z respondents rated 😊 and 👍 as more passive-aggressive than older respondents did, but nobody has measured how any generation reads 🥺 as I miss you.

faqs.question: Is it better to send an emoji or write a sentence?
faqs.answer: Adding words helps less than people expect: a study of 2,482 participants found interpretation stayed about as variable with surrounding text as without it. On our own miss-you pages the median written letter runs 88 words, and the longest is 1,024.

faqs.question: What is a CLDR short name?
faqs.answer: It is the descriptive label your keyboard search and screen reader use for an emoji, published in Unicode's emoji-test.txt. It is not the same string as the formal character name in UnicodeData.txt, and for 🤗 the two disagree: HUGGING FACE against smiling face with open hands.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Miss You Emoji Meaning: Unicode Has Never Encoded One

There is no "miss you" emoji. Unicode has never encoded one. Of the 3,966 fully-qualified emoji sequences in [emoji-test.txt for Unicode 18.0](https://unicode.org/Public/emoji/latest/emoji-test.txt), dated 30 April 2026, not one carries *miss*, *longing*, *lonely*, *yearn* or *nostalgia* in its name. So the real question behind *miss you emoji meaning* is which of 🥺 🫂 💔 😢 😭 🥹 😔 🫰 gets **read** as "I miss you" — a different question with a different answer. The receiving end seems to know this already: recipients of our miss-you pages sent back 1,434 hug taps across 138 of 214 pages, a gesture rather than a word, while the median written letter on those pages runs 88 words. Below: every codepoint, the version each arrived in, what the research says about being understood, and when to stop reaching for a glyph.

## Is there a "miss you" emoji in Unicode?

No. Unicode encodes characters, not sentiments, and no character in the standard is defined as meaning "I miss you". The Consortium publishes the complete list as a plain text file, `emoji-test.txt`, and the current one covers Unicode 18.0.

Search all 3,966 of its CLDR short names for *miss*, *longing*, *lonely*, *yearn* or *nostalgia* and one line comes back: 🪘 **long drum**, a false positive on "long". There is no second hit.

What exists instead is a set of faces and symbols people have pressed into service. Each has an official name, a codepoint and a release version, and none of the three is "miss you".

## Eight emoji people send for "I miss you", and what Unicode calls each

Every name and codepoint below comes from `emoji-test.txt`, every release version from [DerivedAge.txt in the Unicode Character Database](https://www.unicode.org/Public/UCD/latest/ucd/DerivedAge.txt), dated 29 June 2026.

### 1. 🥺 — U+1F97A, pleading face

Unicode 11.0, 2018. CLDR short name *pleading face*; formal character name FACE WITH PLEADING EYES. It means asking, not missing. It reads as "I want something from you" — close enough to longing that it became the default, far enough that it also reads as wheedling.

### 2. 🫂 — U+1FAC2, people hugging

Unicode 13.0, 2020. Two featureless figures: no faces, no gender, no skin tone. It survives being sent to a parent as easily as to a partner, and it is the only one here that depicts what someone missing a person actually wants.

### 3. 💔 — U+1F494, broken heart

Unicode 6.0, 2010, so it renders on essentially any phone still switched on. Its problem is severity: it is the emoji of a breakup and a bereavement as much as of a Tuesday apart, and nothing in it says which you meant.

### 4. 😢 — U+1F622, crying face

Unicode 6.0, 2010. In the Emoji Sentiment Ranking it scores +0.007 across 749 occurrences — indistinguishable from neutral, 39.1% of annotations positive against 38.4% negative. The crying face is not reliably read as sad.

### 5. 😭 — U+1F62D, loudly crying face

Unicode 6.0, 2010. It scores −0.093 over 5,526 occurrences, so it reads as more negative than 😢 despite being the one people reach for when being theatrical. It is by a wide margin the most-used of this group.

### 6. 🥹 — U+1F979, face holding back tears

Unicode 14.0, 2021, the newest face here and the riskiest to send. It is *not* "face with tears of joy" — that is 😂, U+1F602 — a mix-up common enough that machine-written answers to this query have printed the wrong name for it.

### 7. 😔 — U+1F614, pensive face

Unicode 6.0, 2010. The most negative of the group in the sentiment lexicon at −0.146 across 1,205 occurrences, 46.4% of annotations negative. To signal low mood rather than affection, this is the one that lands.

### 8. 🫰 — U+1FAF0, hand with index finger and thumb crossed

Unicode 14.0, 2021. The finger heart. Its official name describes a hand position and says nothing about affection: the meaning is conventional, learned from Korean popular culture, invisible to anyone who has not learned it.

## The official name and the name on your phone are two different strings

Unicode publishes two names per emoji and they are not the same object. `UnicodeData.txt` carries the immutable formal character name — for 🥺, FACE WITH PLEADING EYES. `emoji-test.txt` carries the CLDR short name your keyboard search and screen reader use — for 🥺, *pleading face*.

Usually they differ cosmetically. Sometimes they contradict each other. 🤗 is formally HUGGING FACE, fixed at Unicode 8.0 in 2015 and unchangeable; its CLDR short name is *smiling face with open hands*. One says the gesture is a hug, the other says open palms.

So there is no single authority to appeal to when someone reads your emoji differently from the way you meant it: "the official meaning" is two strings from two processes.

## Why the emoji you pick is not always the emoji they see

Two failures sit between your keyboard and their screen, both invisible to you.

The first is age. 💔 😢 😭 😔 all date to Unicode 6.0 in 2010 and render almost anywhere. 🥺 needs Unicode 11.0 from 2018, 🫂 needs 13.0 from 2020, and 🥹 and 🫰 both need 14.0 from 2021. A phone that stopped taking system updates before its emoji font was refreshed shows a tofu box — a blank rectangle — instead. The message still sends. You never find out.

The second is drawing. The standard fixes the codepoint and the name, not the picture. Apple, Google, Samsung and WhatsApp each draw the same codepoint their own way, and Miller and colleagues at the University of Minnesota showed in [their ICWSM 2016 study of emoji interpretation](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/14757) that when two people rated the **same** rendering, they disagreed on whether its sentiment was positive, neutral or negative 25% of the time. Across platforms the disagreement grows.

## What the research says about being read correctly

The obvious fix — wrap the emoji in words — has been tested and does less than people assume. In a [follow-up study with 2,482 participants](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/14901) published on 3 May 2017, the same group had people interpret emoji in isolation and inside several textual contexts. Miscommunication potential came out roughly the same either way.

Sentiment is measurable, at least for the older characters. The [Emoji Sentiment Ranking v1.0](http://kt.ijs.si/data/Emoji_sentiment_ranking/) is the source of every score above: 751 emoji ranked from 1.6 million tweets in 13 European languages, labelled by 83 annotators. It has one hard limit. Built in 2015, it predates 🥺, 🫂, 🥹 and 🫰, which therefore have no score — the emoji people now reach for first are the least studied.

On generational reading there is one measured result, narrower than the claims made about it. Zhukova and Herring's [2024 survey in *Language@Internet*](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/journals/index.php/li/article/view/40800) found Gen Z respondents rated the smile 😊 and thumbs up 👍 as **more** passive-aggressive than older respondents did, while older respondents rated 🔥 and 💣 more negatively. That is what was tested. Nobody has measured how any generation reads 🥺 as "I miss you".

## How to choose, compared

Four ways of sending the same feeling, and what each guarantees. The last column is our own data from the 214 miss-you pages created since 28 July 2026 — two months of it, which is why no seasonal pattern is claimed here.

| What you send | Needs a font from | Measured interpretation disagreement | Our 214 miss-you pages |
|---|---|---|---|
| One emoji, 🥺 U+1F97A | 2018 (Unicode 11.0) | 25% on identical renderings | 86.4% of pages carry a written memory too |
| An emoji plus a sentence | 2018 (Unicode 11.0) | unchanged by context, N = 2,482 | median letter 88 words, longest 1,024 |
| A recorded voice note | no font needed | not studied | 13.6% of senders, 29 of 214 |
| A page with a hug button | no font needed | one meaning, one action | 1,434 taps across 138 of 214 pages |

Ambiguity is a property of the glyph, not of the sender. Both bottom rows work by taking the glyph out of the path.

## When an emoji is the wrong thing to send

When the other person is already upset, an emoji is the wrong choice, and 💔 is the worst of the eight: it reads as rupture rather than absence. When the relationship is new, 🫰 or 🥹 land as noise for anyone below Unicode 14.0 or outside the culture that taught them. When someone has said plainly that they want words, a picture is an evasion.

A SubhSandesh page is sometimes wrong too. If you are in the same city and can go, go. If their phone renders 🥹 as a box, an animated page may struggle on it. And our 2,417 recorded views of miss-you pages are page views, not unique visitors — one person reopening a page twenty times counts as twenty.

A page earns its place when the message has to be private, or has to outlast a scroll. Miss-you senders are the most private segment we have measured: 43.5% password-protect the page before sharing, against 38.5% platform-wide, and the [private miss-you page](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) is built for that reader. If the trouble is words rather than privacy, [Hold My Hand](https://subhsandesh.in/hold-my-hand) suits this reader better: the recipient holds the screen for sixty seconds and a letter unlocks — one unambiguous gesture instead of a glyph whose meaning depends on their font. Everything else sits in the [full template list](https://subhsandesh.in/templates).

One caveat on our own figures: the 47 city pairs those pages name come from a 15-city picker with a default, so they describe the picker as much as the senders and are not presented here as a choice. The fields senders genuinely chose — password, letter, voice note, reunion date — are the ones quoted above.

## Sources

- Unicode Consortium. "[emoji-test.txt, Unicode Emoji 18.0](https://unicode.org/Public/emoji/latest/emoji-test.txt)." File dated 30 April 2026.
- Unicode Consortium. "[DerivedAge.txt, Unicode Character Database 18.0.0](https://www.unicode.org/Public/UCD/latest/ucd/DerivedAge.txt)." File dated 29 June 2026.
- Miller, H., et al. "['Blissfully Happy' or 'Ready to Fight': Varying Interpretations of Emoji](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/14757)." *Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media* 10(1), 259–268. The AAAI record dates the deposit 4 August 2021; the paper is the ICWSM 2016 proceedings.
- Miller, H., et al. "[Understanding Emoji Ambiguity in Context](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/14901)." *Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media* 11(1), 152–161, 3 May 2017.
- Kralj Novak, P., Smailović, J., Sluban, B., & Mozetič, I. "[Emoji Sentiment Ranking v1.0](http://kt.ijs.si/data/Emoji_sentiment_ranking/)." Jožef Stefan Institute; the page publishes no date, so none is recorded.
- Zhukova, M., & Herring, S. C. "[Benign or Toxic? Differences in Emoji Interpretation by Gender, Generation, and Emoji Type](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/journals/index.php/li/article/view/40800)." *Language@Internet* 22, 20 December 2024. Peer-reviewed, open access.

structuralLimitations: THE FRAMING CLAIM IN THE TASK PROMPT IS RIGHT ON THE CENTRAL FACT AND WRONG ON ONE DETAIL, and the detail turned out to be the post's third-best section. The prompt said to 'give the exact codepoint and CLDR short name for every emoji you print — e.g. U+1F97A PLEADING FACE', treating the official name and the CLDR short name as one string. They are two strings from two different processes. UnicodeData.txt gives U+1F97A the immutable formal character name FACE WITH PLEADING EYES; emoji-test.txt gives it the CLDR short name 'pleading face'. For 🤗 U+1F917 they disagree outright: formal name HUGGING FACE, CLDR short name 'smiling face with open hands'. Both files were fetched and parsed in this session. The post prints both names where they differ and devotes an H2 to the divergence, because 'what is the official meaning' has two answers and that is the honest one.

THE CENTRAL FACT IS NOT ASSERTED, IT IS MEASURED. emoji-test.txt for Unicode 18.0 (header dated 2026-04-30) was parsed in full: 3,966 fully-qualified emoji sequences. A regex over every CLDR short name for miss / longing / lonely / yearn / nostalgia returns one line, 🪘 long drum, which is a false positive on the substring 'long'. That is the claim in the H1 and it is reproducible from the cited file in one command.

CANNIBALISATION — BOTH LIVE SLUGS WERE FETCHED AND READ BEFORE DRAFTING, AND NO MERGE IS RECOMMENDED. /blog/i-miss-you-message (~5,800 rendered words) mentions emoji twice, both times as advice ('a photo beats empty emoji', 'avoid using too many'). /blog/cute-ways-to-say-i-miss-you-over-text (~7,900 words) mentions emoji four times, once as an example line ('Miss you ❤️'). Neither names a single emoji formally, gives a codepoint, gives a Unicode version, distinguishes a formal name from a CLDR short name, or cites any research on emoji interpretation. Both are message listicles organised by relationship and tone — 120+ and 70+ lines. This post is about the GLYPH; those are about the SENTENCE. The overlap is the word 'miss' and nothing else, so the honest difference is real: this post adds the Unicode layer (codepoints, release versions, tofu failure), the interpretation-research layer (Miller 2016/2017, the Emoji Sentiment Ranking, Zhukova & Herring 2024) and the recipient-side first-party layer (1,434 hug taps). It does not repeat their message lines and prints none.

THE SIBLING'S PLOS FINDING IS NOT CONTRADICTED AND NOT RE-CITED. say-i-miss-you-without-saying-it publishes the 2025 PLOS One result that perceived responsiveness did NOT significantly predict likability (b = 0.18, p = .10). This post makes no claim of the 'add an emoji and they will like you more' kind in any form — its whole argument runs the other way, that a glyph is an unreliable carrier. journals.plos.org stood at 2 of 3 posts when capcheck was first run and the coordinator's mid-task update confirmed it is now the last slot in the batch; no claim here needs it, so the slot was deliberately left for another agent. Emoji research is concentrated in PLOS ONE, which made this a real constraint rather than a formality; it was met by going to ICWSM (ojs.aaai.org), Language@Internet (scholarworks.iu.edu) and the Jožef Stefan Institute lexicon instead. The peer-reviewed open-access requirement is satisfied three times over without PLOS, so nothing was dropped for the cap.

SERP RUN, NOT PREDICTED — AND THE ENGINE'S OWN SUMMARY GOT AN OFFICIAL NAME WRONG. One WebSearch on the exact keyword on 2026-09-25 returned: emojipedia.org/search (treated as a competitor page per the task brief, not read, not cited, not paraphrased), a TikTok discover page, a Pinterest pin, three copy-paste emoji farms (emoj.info, emojis.wiki, emojicombos.com) and four Wikipedia pages, three of which are about a song or a disambiguation and answer nothing. No AI Overview or featured snippet was returned in the result set, and no unicode.org result appears anywhere on page one. The synthesis generated from those pages called 🥹 'face with tear of joy'; 🥹 is U+1F979 FACE HOLDING BACK TEARS, and 'face with tears of joy' is 😂 U+1F602. That mis-naming is cited inside the post as evidence of the gap.

NO CLAIM IS MADE ABOUT WHAT ANY EMOJI MEANS TO GEN Z BEYOND WHAT WAS MEASURED. Zhukova & Herring (2024) tested 😊 👍 🔥 💣 and found Gen Z respondents rated the smile and thumbs up as more passive-aggressive than older respondents did. That is exactly what the post reports, and the post then states plainly that nobody has measured how any generation reads 🥺 as 'I miss you'. The folk-wisdom genre this keyword usually attracts is named and refused rather than reproduced.

ABSTRACT-ONLY READING IS DISCLOSED FOR THREE SOURCES. For Miller et al. 2016, Miller et al. 2017 and Zhukova & Herring 2024 the publisher abstract and bibliographic record were read in full; the PDFs were not opened. Every figure quoted from those three (25% polarity disagreement, N = 2,482 and the no-support-for-context finding, the Gen Z passive-aggression result) is stated verbatim in the abstract, so nothing is inferred beyond it. None of the three is paywalled — all are open access — so the checklist's paywall clause does not bite, but the limitation is recorded here rather than left implicit.

THE MILLER 2016 DATE IS THE PUBLISHER'S, NOT THE CONFERENCE'S. The AAAI OJS record for '“Blissfully Happy” or “Ready to Fight”' states Published: 2021-08-04 and its own suggested citation reads (2021), although the paper is the ICWSM 2016 proceedings paper, vol. 10(1), 259–268. batchMeta.sources and the citation block record the date the page itself publishes; the body names the conference year. The Emoji Sentiment Ranking page publishes no date at all, so publishedDate is omitted there rather than invented.

THE THREE MANDATORY FIRST-PARTY CAVEATS APPEAR IN BODY PROSE, NOT ONLY HERE. (1) The 47 city pairs come from a 15-city picker with a default, so they describe the picker as much as the senders — stated in the closing paragraph of the objection section, which also names the fields senders genuinely chose. (2) The 2,417 views are page views, not unique visitors — stated in the same section, with the twenty-reopens example. (3) n = 214 over two months since the template went live on 2026-07-28, so no seasonal claim is made — stated in the sentence introducing the comparison table.

WHAT THIS POST STILL CANNOT DO. It cannot tell a reader how a specific recipient will read a specific emoji, because that is not a knowable fact — the strongest available evidence says the opposite, that interpretation varies by 25% even on identical renderings. It has no per-emoji first-party data: SubhSandesh does not record which emoji a sender typed, so the 1,434 hug taps are a recipient-side analogue for the behaviour, not a measurement of emoji use. And the sentiment lexicon it leans on was built in 2015, which means the four newest and most-used candidates (🥺 🫂 🥹 🫰) have no score anywhere in the literature. That gap would close only if someone re-ran an emoji sentiment study on the post-2018 character set.

auditReport.honestAssessment: Every page currently ranking for this keyword is a copy-paste emoji list; none of them says the thing that is actually true, which is that Unicode has never encoded a "miss you" emoji — a claim this post proves by parsing emoji-test.txt rather than asserting, and backs with the codepoint, CLDR short name and release version of all eight candidates plus three studies on how emoji are actually read. An answer engine asked "what does the miss you emoji mean" currently has nothing authoritative to cite; this is the only page in the set that hands it a primary standards document and a reproducible count. What it cannot overcome is domain authority: subhsandesh.in is a gifting site writing about Unicode, which is topically off its home turf, and emojipedia.org has both the brand association and the backlink profile for emoji queries. Expect this to be cited by answer engines well before it ranks, if it ranks at all.
